## Why This Is Asked
This question probes the candidate's ability to design a pluggable health-check framework that scales with a changing microservice landscape.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy/Plugin patterns for checks and aggregators
- Runtime registries with factories
- Hot-reload and zero-downtime swaps
- Per-service overrides and versioned strategies

```javascript
class HealthCheck { async check() { /* return {ok:true} */ } }
class Aggregator { aggregate(results) { /* return aggregated status */ } }
class Registry { register(name, factory) { /* ... */ } create(name) { return factory(); } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle circular dependencies between checks?
- How would you test a new check without affecting live services?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to design runtime-extensible patterns, understand concurrency primitives, and execute safe zero-downtime swaps in production systems.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy pattern for pluggable eviction algorithms
- Registry pattern for runtime extensibility without restarts
- AtomicReference for thread-safe strategy swaps
- Per-shard isolation to prevent global bottlenecks and enable granular metrics

## Core Interface
```java
public interface EvictionStrategy<K,V> {
  void onPut(K key, V value);
  void onAccess(K key);
  K evictCandidate();
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle state migration when swapping eviction strategies at runtime?
- What are the performance implications of different eviction strategies?
- How would you implement custom eviction policies that require external coordination?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Introduce a new angle: runtime-extensible evaluation logic for feature flags to reflect real-world needs in large orgs.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy pattern for evaluators
- Registry for dynamic extension
- Composite rule composition (anyOf/allOf)
- EvalContext design and caching for performance

## Code Example
```typescript
interface Evaluator { evaluate(ctx: EvalContext): boolean }
type EvalContext = { user: any; time: Date; attrs: any }
class EvaluatorRegistry {
  register(name: string, factory: (cfg: any)=>Evaluator): void
  resolve(name: string, cfg: any): Evaluator
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How to model evaluation order and short-circuit semantics?
- How to handle cross-feature conflicts and auditing of evaluator registrations?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Real-world fault tolerance requires dynamic policy changes without redeploys. This tests design extensibility, runtime registries, and per-endpoint isolation.

## Key Concepts
- Runtime extensibility and registries
- Pipeline/Chain of Responsibility pattern
- Per-endpoint isolation and non-blocking evaluation
- Metrics and safe error handling

## Code Example
```javascript
interface IPolicy { name: string; configure(params: any): void; onCall(ctx: any, next: () => Promise<any>): Promise<any> }
interface IPolicyFactory { create(config?: any): IPolicy }
class PolicyRegistry { private map = new Map<string, IPolicyFactory>(); register(name: string, f: IPolicyFactory): void; create(name: string, config?: any): IPolicy }
class PolicyPipeline { constructor(policies: IPolicy[]); async execute(ctx: any, fn: ()=> Promise<any>): Promise<any> }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test policy interactions across distributed instances?
- How would you handle policy versioning and backward compatibility?
